title: Unexpected routing surge from late capacity signals — postmortem and remediation
creator: Leah Kim
description:
Summary:
On 2026-03-01 03:14 UTC we observed a sudden spike in fallbacks and tail latency for a subset of traffic routed through the eu-west region. Traffic that should have been steered away by a draining policy instead continued to be routed to a partially drained pool, triggering a cascade: the degraded region began timing out, the routing control plane simultaneously issued broad fallback decisions to compatible model variants, and those variants were overloaded leading to higher latencies and a visible error spike for affected customers.

Impact:
- Duration: ~35 minutes of elevated errors and increased latency (03:14–03:49 UTC).
- Affected surface: 12% of host traffic for the EU tenant cluster; 7 customer accounts reported increased 5xx rates (one enterprise with tight SLOs).
- Observable metrics: 4x increase in 5xx, median token latency for affected routes rose from 110ms to 520ms, model-variant queue lengths doubled.

Timeline (abridged):
- 03:10 UTC: Autoscaling event started for eu-west pool; operator initiated a manual drain to decommission a node for maintenance.
- 03:12 UTC: Control plane marked the node as draining and wrote a drain flag to the regional discovery layer. The drain flag propagation was subject to two caches: the control-plane cache (TTL 2s) and the routing-proxy local cache (TTL 30s).
- 03:14 UTC: A batch of long-running requests resumed from clients; routing proxies with stale local caches (TTL not refreshed due to a bug) continued sending new inflight requests to the draining node.
- 03:15 UTC: Draining node began exhibiting elevated queuing; health-checks tripped intermittently. Control plane attempted automated fallbacks to variant B (smaller, quantized) and to a different region when capacity signals degraded.
- 03:16–03:25 UTC: Fallback controller performed aggressive variant substitution (no rate limiting). Variant B pools hit concurrency limits and CPU bound tails increased. Fallback ramp lacked a circuit-breaker and exhausted capacity in other pools, producing a cascading failure.
- 03:25 UTC: On-call noticed alerts and started manual mitigation: paused automated fallback policy and re-routed traffic away from eu-west to eu-central.
- 03:49 UTC: Metrics returned to baseline after traffic redistribution and transient autoscaling completed.

Root causes (multi-factor):
1) Control-plane -> proxy cache mismatch: the routing proxies used a 30s local cache for region/tier drain flags; due to a bug in the cache-refresh path that skipped invalidation on event reconciliation, several proxies kept stale drain state and continued directing new requests to nodes marked draining.
2) Fallback controller lacking rate-limits and circuit-breakers: automated fallback policy applied variant swaps globally without progressive rollout or capacity checks, amplifying load on replacement pools (no per-variant concurrency gating).
3) Observability gap for early signal: the capacity anomaly detector was tuned for absolute error spikes but not for subtle concurrency pressure on variant pools; by the time the detector fired, overload had propagated.

Contributing factors:
- Maintenance window overlapped with a traffic burst (client retry pattern).
- Recent change in discovery-layer (PR #8421) increased cache TTLs in proxies to reduce control-plane chatter; this change had inadequate test coverage for drain propagation scenarios.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident:
- Disabled automated global fallback policy (03:20 UTC).
- Forced full cache invalidation across all routing proxies for eu-west (03:22 UTC).
- Applied emergency rate-limit on variant B pools (03:23 UTC).
- Re-routed non-critical routes to fallback regions (03:26 UTC).

Permanent fixes and planned work (owner + ETA):
- Short term (1 week):
  - ENGR-1: Reduce routing-proxy local cache TTL from 30s -> 2s and add mandatory invalidation on drain events (owner: Omar Patel; ETA: 2026-03-08).
  - ENGR-2: Add optimistic cache-reconciliation that forces a full fetch on discovery-layer heartbeats after maintenance events (owner: Maya Singh; ETA: 2026-03-07).
  - ENGR-3: Add per-variant concurrency circuit-breaker to fallback controller (owner: Carlos Romero; ETA: 2026-03-10).
- Medium term (1–2 months):
  - ENGR-4: Expand capacity anomaly detector to watch derivative metrics (queue growth rate, median queue wait time) and surface early warning (owner: Priya Rao; ETA: 2026-04-15).
  - ENGR-5: Implement progressive, capacity-aware fallback rollouts (gradual percentage-based substitution with backoff on errors) (owner: Omar Patel; ETA: 2026-04-01).
- Long term (quarter):
  - ENGR-6: Simulation harness for drain scenarios at scale to validate cache, fallback, and autoscaling interactions (owner: SRE; ETA: 2026-Q2).

Telemetry and dashboards changes:
- New dashboard panels: variant pool queue depth (per-region), drain-flag propagation latency, fallback substitution rate. (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/9056)
- Alert tuning: lower sensitivity threshold for derivative queue growth alerts; add a paging alert for fallback substitution rate > 100rps sustained for 1 minute.

PRs, runbooks, and artifacts:
- Root cause PRs: discovery: https://github.com/redwood-inference/discovery/pull/8421 (cache change), proxy invalidation fix: https://github.com/redwood-inference/proxy/pull/2283, fallback controller circuit-breaker: https://github.com/redwood-inference/controller/pull/3167.
- Incident runbook updates: https://confluence.redwood.ai/routing/incident-playbooks#drain-fallback (added steps to force cache invalidation and to throttle fallbacks).
- Dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rt-routing/routing-resilience

Post-incident notes & action items assigned during review meeting (2026-03-05):
- Validate proxy cache TTL reduction in a canary region before cluster-wide rollout (task: ENG-20090).
- Add a staged fallback experiment harness to our integration test suite that simulates node drains under realistic client retry patterns (task: ENG-20110).
- Run a tabletop exercise for on-call and control-plane engineers to practice coordinated drain + fallback incidents (owner: SRE lead; scheduled: 2026-03-22).

Lessons learned (short):
- Small configuration tweaks (cache TTL) can have outsized cascade effects when combined with automation that assumes immediate propagation.
- Fallbacks need to be capacity-aware and gradual; automated substitutions without gating create single points of failure.
- Observability should include early derivative signals (queue growth) in addition to absolute error counts.

Reviewer notes and approvals:
- Reviewed by: Product (Aisha Thompson), SRE (Daniel Wu), Security (N/A), Engineering Leads (Maya Singh, Carlos Romero).
- Postmortem accepted: 2026-03-10.

Follow-ups (for tracking):
- ENG-20090 (canary and rollout for cache TTL) — owner: Omar Patel — due 2026-03-08.
- ENG-20110 (fallback experiment harness) — owner: Priya Rao — due 2026-04-01.
- ENG-20150 (anomaly detector expansion) — owner: Priya Rao — due 2026-04-15.
